blocks.text: VI. The sixth passage, Iob. XXXVIII, 36., reads thus in Hebrew: Who has put בטחות wisdom in the reins, or given לשכוי understanding to the heart? In Scripture, namely, heart and reins are frequently joined, as being, in the mind of the Hebrews, the proper seat of thoughts. For examples see Psalm. VII, 10. and XXVI, 2. and LXXIII, 21., Proverb. XXIII, 15. 26. Ierem. XI, 20. and XVII, 10. and XX, 12. So also in this passage. But whereas the reins are commonly called כליות and the heart לב, here each is given another name, and a more poetic one. The reins are called טוחות tuchoth [col. 115] here and in Psal. LI, 8., from the verb טוח, which means to smear and to coat, because the reins are smeared and coated with fat, as has already been proved elsewhere. The heart, on the other hand, is called שכוי, from the verb שכה, which means to think and to imagine. Hence also שכיות are pictures and images, Es. II, 16., and אבן משכית is a painted stone, Levit. XXVI, 1.; and משכיות לבב, imaginations of the heart, Psal. LXXIII, 7.; and במשכיתו, in his imagination, Prov. XVIII, 11. Although these things are clear and plain, and confirmed in explicit words by the most learned of the Hebrews, namely Kimchi, Aben Ezra and R. Levi, others have nevertheless chosen to interpret the words of Job just cited thus: Who has put wisdom in the reins, or given understanding to the cock? As if שכוי in that place meant cock. The first author of this fiction was a certain R. Simeon, son of Lakis, whose words are cited as follows in the Talmudic tractate On the beginning of the year, fol. 26a: כשהלכתי לתחום קן נשריא הוו קורין לכלה נינפי ולתרנגול שכוי, When I was travelling through the territory of Kennasaria, there they called a bride nympha, and a cock secui. In the same place others trifle that a bride is called nympha because Mount Zion is called beautiful in נוף noph, that is, in situation, Psal. XLVIII, 3. (For the Greek word νύμφη [nymphē] escaped these circumcised doctors.) They add that the cock is called שכוי secui from the passage of Job we have mentioned. From so impure a source the error at once spread more widely and found many defenders. Among them the Chaldee translator gives a twofold interpretation of this passage: one sound and true, מן יהב ללבא בינתא, Who gave understanding to the heart?; the other Talmudic, מן יהב לתרנגולא ברא בינתא למקלסא למרה, Who gave the wild cock understanding, to praise his Lord? And R. Selomo asserts both thus: למכוי זה תרנגול לשון חכמים וי״א הלב, Secui in the language of the sages means cock, although others explain it as heart. And Aquinas, after quoting the passage of Job: יש מפרשים תרנגול והוא שגור מאד במשנה, There are some who interpret it as cock, which is very common in the Mishnah. Kimchi proves this at some length, although he [II, 683] is of the other opinion. Accordingly, in the Prayer Book, printed and reprinted so many times, this prayer is found among the morning prayers: בא״י אמ״ה אשר נתן לשכוי בינה להבין בין יום ובין לילה, Blessed art thou, O Lord our God, King of the world, who hast given τῷ [tō] secui (that is, the cock) understanding to distinguish day from night. In this prayer the allusion to the passage of Job is evident. And Jerome, no doubt persuaded by that Jew whom he had as his teacher, rendered the same passage thus: Who has put wisdom in the inward parts of man? or who has given understanding to the cock? He thus joins in the same verse two ἀσύνδετα [asyndeta], namely the wisdom of man with the natural instinct of the cock, by which it is prompted to crow at fixed hours. And this in a book in which the two hemistichs of a verse are almost always ἀντίστροφα [antistropha]. I shall note in passing the origin of the version of the Greeks, which might seem entirely foreign: Τίς δὲ ἔδωκεν γυναιξὶν ὑφάσματος σοφίαν, ἢ ποικιλτικὴν ἐπιστήμην; [Tis de edōken gynaixin hyphasmatos sophian, ē poikiltikēn epistēmēn?] And who gave women wisdom in weaving, or skill in embroidery? For בטחות, in the reins, they read בטוות, in spinning women; and לשכות, for painting or variegating, for לשכוי, to the heart. Written that way, the Hebrew is rendered word for word: Who has put wisdom in spinning women? Or who has given them understanding for painting, or variegating? But the Greek translators turned the skill of spinning into ὑφάσματος σοφίαν [hyphasmatos sophian], because νῆμα [nēma] and ὕφασμα [hyphasma] are often used interchangeably, as it would be easy to prove from Homer, Hesychius and Eustathius.

VII. The seventh passage, Iob. XXXIX, 13. (var. 16.), כנף רננים נעלסה, is rendered thus by the Chaldee: גדפא דתרנגולא דמשבחא ומקלסא, The wing of the cock, which praises and [col. 116] celebrates. They refer this to the cock discussed above. But in the chapter On the Ostrich we have proved at length that these words must be rendered thus: The wing of the ostriches exults. Accordingly this passage too is beside the point.
